successor: Australian administration of Papua (military rule/ANGAU from Feb 1942; later Territory of Papua and New Guinea)
source1: H. N. Nelson, 'Murray, Hubert Leonard (1886-1963)', Australian Dictionary of Biography vol. 15, Melbourne University Press 2000 - https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/murray-hubert-leonard-11208
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Papua New Guinea: The colonial period' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Papua-New-Guinea/The-colonial-period
notes: Australian cabinet ended Papua's civil administration; military rule declared 14 Feb 1942. Japanese advance stopped short of Port Moresby (core), so Australian authority continued, later as Territory of Papua and New Guinea. Japanese occupation of Buna-Gona was outside the core.

successor: Frankish kingdom under Carolingian kings (Carolingian Empire I)
notes: Pippinid mayors already held de facto power over the regnum Francorum; in 751 Pippin III deposed Childeric III and was elected king, a dynastic change within the same Frankish state. Neustrian revolt after 714; peripheral-duchy insurrections in 740s.

successor: First Turk Khaganate (Sogdiana; Sasanians south of the Oxus)
source1: A. D. H. Bivar, 'Hephthalites', Encyclopaedia Iranica, 2003 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/hephthalites
notes: Khosrow I and the Turks crushed the Hephthalites near Bukhara c. 558-561 and divided their lands along the Oxus; Turks took Sogdiana. Rump Hephthalite principalities survived in Afghanistan. Capital at end uncertain; no documented internal crisis.

source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Mali Empire' essay - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/mali/hd_mali.htm
notes: No break c. 1410: Gao revolted c. 1400 and Tuareg took Timbuktu/Walata 1431, yet Mali persisted, ceasing to matter politically c. 1550 and shrinking to its heartland by 1645. Database end date is an artefact.

successor: uncertain: reduced Knossos and a separate Kydonia (Chania) kingdom (Postpalatial Crete)
source1: Jeremy B. Rutter, Aegean Prehistoric Archaeology, Lesson 18 narrative, Dartmouth College - https://sites.dartmouth.edu/aegean-prehistory/lessons/lesson-18-narrative/
source2: Birgitta P. Hallager, LM IIIB Knossos and its relations to Kydonia (Acta Instituti Atheniensis Regni Sueciae 4o, 61), Swedish Institute at Athens 2025, publisher description - https://ecsi.se/actaath-4-61/
notes: Knossos palace burned c. 1375 BCE (early LM IIIA2) through human agency, perpetrators unknown (mainland Mycenaeans or Minoan revolt); it may have functioned into LM IIIB beside a separate Kydonia kingdom. Mode and date unresolved.

source2: Muhammad Maysar Muhammad Bahauddin, 'The Rasulid State in Yemen (626-858 AH/1229-1454 AD): origins and political conditions', University of Mosul conference special issue, 2022 - https://berj.uomosul.edu.iq/index.php/berj/article/download/38143/37928/38233
notes: After 1442 the Rasulids' own mamluk troops made and unmade sultans; the last sultan, unable to retake Zabid, abdicated at Ta'izz in 1454. The Tahirids, magnates within the realm, rose on its ruins: internal takeover, no external conquest.

successor: Odoacer's Kingdom of Italy (476-493), conquered by the Ostrogoths 489-493
notes: 476: Odoacer, commander of Italy's federate troops (internal), deposed Romulus Augustulus, keeping the administration and Senate. Within W, Theodoric's Ostrogoths from Moesia (external) conquered Italy 489-493, taking Ravenna; priority rule gives T2. Orestes' coup preceded.

successor: Deva dynasty of south-east Bengal (Vikramapura); Turkish rulers held west Bengal from 1204
source2: A. M. Chowdhury, 'Sena Dynasty', Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh - https://en.banglapedia.org/index.php/Sena_Dynasty
notes: Bakhtiyar Khalji expelled Lakshmanasena from Nadia 1202/1204; descendants ruled Vanga/Vikramapura to at least 1245, then the Devas of south-east Bengal supplanted them. Conquest inferred, not documented. Independent chiefs had fragmented the realm.

successor: Elam II (Neo-Elamite kingdom under Humban-nikash I)
source1: Francois Vallat, 'Elam i. The history of Elam', Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/3, 1998 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-i
source2: Elizabeth Carter, 'Elam ii. The archeology of Elam', Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/3 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-ii
notes: 743 BCE is Humban-nikash I's accession, when Babylonian Chronicle coverage begins; nothing indicates a break. Kings kept the title of Anshan and Susa, and Susa revived in the late 8th century. Pre-743 Elam is undocumented, so crisis unknown.

source1: Ulrich Theobald, 'The Regional State of Wei', ChinaKnowledge.de, 2018 - http://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Zhou/rulers-wei.html
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'China: The Qin empire (221-207 BCE)' (Qin unification of rival states and prefecture-county system) - https://www.britannica.com/place/China/The-Qin-empire-221-207-bce
notes: Qin general Wang Ben flooded the capital Daliang c. 225 BCE; King Jia was Wei's last ruler and Wei became a Qin commandery. Candidate successor Western Han is wrong; Qin held the core. No documented internal crisis.
